questions.prompt: When Darcy asks to be introduced to her companions, Elizabeth expects him to “decamp.” What happens instead, and why does she feel triumph?
facilitatorNotes: He is surprised to learn they are her relations but “sustained it, however, with fortitude,” turns back with them, talks with Mr. Gardiner and invites him to fish. Elizabeth “gloried” in her uncle’s good sense and manners.
Her triumph is double: Darcy behaves well, and her family is shown to have members “for whom there was no need to blush.” Ask how this answers his proposal speech.
evidence: he sustained it, however, with fortitude
It was consoling that he should know she had some relations for whom there was no need to blush.

questions.prompt: “It cannot be for me … It is impossible that he should still love me.” How does the walk test that statement?
facilitatorNotes: He explains his early arrival, mentions Bingley’s coming, and asks to introduce his sister, “a compliment of the highest kind.” Then they stand on the lawn talking of Matlock and Dovedale “with great perseverance” because no real subject feels safe.
Her denial is part hope: she repeats it as if to stop herself believing otherwise. Some readers take the awkward silence as proof of feeling on both sides.
evidence: It is impossible that he should still love me.
His wish of introducing his sister to her was a compliment of the highest kind.
they talked of Matlock and Dovedale with great perseverance

questions.prompt: The Gardiners now judge Darcy from one morning. What do they get right, what do they get wrong, and why does Elizabeth speak up for him?
facilitatorNotes: They find him “perfectly well-behaved, polite, and unassuming” but suspect his civility is “whimsical,” and Mrs. Gardiner still credits Wickham’s story and laughs at the housekeeper’s “flaming character.”

Elizabeth, “in as guarded a manner as she could,” corrects the record about the money dealings without naming Darcy’s letter. Ask why she does it now, when she and Jane chose silence in Hertfordshire.
evidence: He is perfectly well-behaved, polite, and unassuming
But perhaps he may be a little whimsical in his civilities
in as guarded a manner as she could

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Georgiana Darcy, and a sleepless night
readings.challenge: Read the visit through three sets of watchers, then follow Elizabeth’s long night of sorting out her feelings word by word.
readings.focus: A shy sister, a hopeful Bingley and an altered Darcy; Elizabeth names what she feels, from respect to gratitude, and stops short of love.
readings.context: Recap: at Pemberley Elizabeth met Darcy by surprise. He was courteous to her uncle and aunt, the merchant relations he once despised, and asked to introduce his sister, Georgiana, who is about sixteen. Mr. Bingley, who left Jane last autumn on Darcy’s advice, is staying at Pemberley with his sisters; Miss Bingley had hoped to marry Darcy and had pictured Georgiana as Bingley’s future wife. A curricle is a light two-wheeled carriage; livery is the uniform colours of a household’s servants.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XLIV, complete; opens “ELIZABETH had settled it that Mr. Darcy would bring his sister to visit her the very day…”; closes “…and a positive engagement made of his meeting some of the gentlemen at Pemberley by noon.”.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth expected Miss Darcy to be proud. What does she find, and what does the mistake suggest about first impressions?
facilitatorNotes: Georgiana is “exceedingly shy,” not proud, and hardly speaks “beyond a monosyllable”; “sense and good-humour” are in her face. Elizabeth had heard otherwise in Lambton.
The reversal echoes the whole novel: reserve can look like pride. Ask who else in the book has been misjudged this way.
evidence: she had heard that Miss Darcy was exceedingly proud; but the observation of a very few minutes convinced her that she was only exceedingly shy

questions.prompt: What signs of Jane does Elizabeth find in Bingley’s behaviour? How sure can she be of them?
facilitatorNotes: He shows no special regard for Miss Darcy; he says it is “above eight months” since they met and names “the 26th of November”; he asks whether all her sisters are at Longbourn.
The narrator warns that “this might be imaginary” and calls her reading “anxious interpretation.” The exact date is the strongest evidence, but Elizabeth wants to find it.
evidence: We have not met since the 26th of November, when we were all dancing together at Netherfield.
in her anxious interpretation

questions.prompt: How do the Gardiners interpret Darcy, and how do they treat what they have guessed?
facilitatorNotes: They decide that “one of them at least knew what it was to love” and that he is “very much in love with her,” but they do not press Elizabeth: they saw “nothing to justify inquiry.” They also now have “an interest” in believing the housekeeper.
They are tactful and fair-minded, which matters after Darcy’s scorn for them. Ask whether their wish to think well of him makes their judgment less reliable.
evidence: one of them at least knew what it was to love
They saw much to interest, but nothing to justify inquiry.
There was now an interest, however, in believing the housekeeper

questions.prompt: In the long paragraph about her sleepless night, Elizabeth moves through several feelings. Put them in order. Why is gratitude the one the narrator dwells on?
facilitatorNotes: Hatred is gone; then respect, esteem, a “friendlier” feeling, and “above all” gratitude, for his loving her “still well enough to forgive” her rejection. She ends wanting to know “how far she wished that welfare to depend upon herself.”
Gratitude responds to his change and her own past injustice; it is not yet love. Some readers think Austen is cautious about sudden passion; others hear love just beneath the careful words.
evidence: She certainly did not hate him.
It was gratitude;—gratitude, not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still well enough to forgive all the petulance and acrimony of her manner in rejecting him
she only wanted to know how far she wished that welfare to depend upon herself

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Miss Bingley’s attack
readings.challenge: Watch a scene of politeness used as a weapon. Track who knows what about Wickham, and how that changes the meaning of one question.
readings.focus: Miss Bingley’s jealous civility backfires twice, and Darcy finally says plainly what he thinks of Elizabeth.
readings.context: Recap: Darcy has brought his shy sister Georgiana to meet Elizabeth at the inn in Lambton, and the Gardiners have guessed that he loves her. Elizabeth now calls at Pemberley with her aunt. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley are Bingley’s sisters; Miss Bingley has long hoped to marry Darcy and has always mocked Elizabeth. Mrs. Annesley is Georgiana’s companion. Only Darcy, Georgiana and Elizabeth know of Georgiana’s near-elopement with Wickham. Novels of the time often printed a dash in place of a real county’s name, as in “——shire.”

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XLV, complete; opens “CONVINCED as Elizabeth now was that Miss Bingley’s dislike of her had originated in…”; closes “…and Mrs. Gardiner would have been highly gratified by her niece’s beginning the subject.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Annesley show that she is “more truly well-bred” than the Bingley sisters?
facilitatorNotes: She breaks the awkward silence and keeps the conversation going with Mrs. Gardiner, while the sisters give only a curtsy, and Miss Bingley asks one “cold inquiry.” She also prompts Georgiana with looks to serve the refreshments.
Austen measures good breeding by effort to put others at ease, not by rank. Ask how this fits the earlier contrast between Pemberley’s housekeeper and Elizabeth’s expectations.
evidence: whose endeavour to introduce some kind of discourse proved her to be more truly well-bred than either of the others
a cold inquiry after the health of her family

questions.prompt: Miss Bingley asks about the ——shire militia. What does she intend, and what does she actually do?
facilitatorNotes: She means to embarrass Elizabeth by recalling Wickham and her family’s follies with the officers. But she does not know about Georgiana’s near-elopement, so the hint wounds Georgiana and Darcy instead.
The narrator spells out the dramatic irony: “Had Miss Bingley known what pain she was then giving her beloved friend.” Elizabeth’s calm answer turns the attack into a credit to her.
evidence: Pray, Miss Eliza, are not the ——shire militia removed from Meryton?
Not a syllable had ever reached her of Miss Darcy’s meditated elopement.

questions.prompt: Look at Miss Bingley’s catalogue of Elizabeth’s face. What does its detail reveal about the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: She lists face, complexion, features, nose, teeth and eyes, finding fault with each, ending with “a self-sufficiency without fashion.” The length and care show how much she has studied her rival.
The narrator’s comment, “angry people are not always wise,” turns the speech against her. Students might compare it with Darcy’s first remark about Elizabeth at the Meryton ball.
evidence: Her nose wants character; there is nothing marked in its lines.
angry people are not always wise

questions.prompt: Darcy finally replies “one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance.” Why does Austen end the scene with Miss Bingley’s “satisfaction,” and then with the drive home?
facilitatorNotes: Miss Bingley forced the remark that “gave no one any pain but herself”: the word “satisfaction” is ironic. In the carriage, aunt and niece discuss “everything but himself.”
The silence in the carriage is as telling as Darcy’s speech. Ask why neither woman will start the subject they both care about.
evidence: for it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance
Miss Bingley was left to all the satisfaction of having forced him to say what gave no one any pain but herself
They talked of his sister, his friends, his house, his fruit, of everything but himself
